name: Ad-tech — frequency capping & pacing
parent_research_topic: Beava use cases — current and potential applications of beava as a real-time feature server

domain_fit.domain_name: Ad-tech frequency capping and budget pacing (DSP / SSP / exchange / CTV ad-server)
domain_fit.one_line_definition: A DSP, SSP, ad exchange or CTV ad-server decides on every bid request — within a single-digit-ms slice of an industry-wide ~100 ms RTB budget — whether to bid / serve a given creative to a given (user-or-household, campaign, creative) tuple, by consulting per-tuple impression counters (frequency caps) and per-campaign delivery-rate features (pacing).
domain_fit.representative_jobs_to_be_done: 1) Enforce per-user-per-campaign (and per-creative, per-line-item, per-household for CTV) impression caps in real time on every bid / ad-select decision, with strict no-double-count so the buyer doesn't over-deliver and breach an IO. 2) Drive a pacing feedback loop (smooth vs ASAP vs front-load) by exposing per-campaign spend-rate, impression-rate and win-rate features that a separate pacing controller (PID / multiplicative / bang-bang) reads every 1-10 s and converts into a bid-price multiplier or a throttling probability. 3) Feed pCTR / pCVR scorers with the same per-(user × campaign × creative) recency, count and velocity features so ranking, capping and pacing all see one consistent view of state.
domain_fit.event_shapes: bid_request {ts, bid_id, user_id_or_household_id, campaign_id, creative_id, line_item_id, exchange, geo, device, k_anon_ok?}, bid_win / win_notice {ts, bid_id, price_paid, win_ts, exchange}, impression / billable_imp {ts, bid_id, user_id, campaign_id, creative_id, billable, rendered}, click {ts, bid_id, user_id, campaign_id}, conversion / postback {ts, user_id, campaign_id, value, attributed_bid_id}, viewable_imp {ts, bid_id, mrc_50_1s_or_2s}, budget_update {ts, campaign_id, daily_budget, lifetime_budget, pacing_mode}. The beava/python/beava/demos/adtech demo already ships Impression / Click / Conversion events with (user_id, campaign_id) keys — directly the right shape for this domain.
domain_fit.feature_shapes: Frequency-capping side (counter / velocity primitives): count(impression) per (user × campaign) in 1h / 24h / 7d / lifetime tumbling+sliding windows; count(impression) per (household × campaign) for CTV; count(impression) per (user × creative); recency / time-since-last-impression per (user × campaign) for n-per-hour recency caps; n_unique(creative_id) seen per user per campaign for creative rotation. Pacing side (rate / distribution / velocity primitives): velocity(impressions) and velocity(spend) per campaign over short (10 s / 1 min) and long (1 h / 24 h) windows; rate(spend / budget_remaining); distribution(price_paid) for floor / second-price diagnostics; win_rate = wins / bids per campaign per minute. Scoring-side: same per-(user × campaign) features feed pCTR / pCVR alongside campaign-level historical rates.
domain_fit.entity_grain: Composite and high-cardinality. Primary keys: user_id (or graph-resolved cross-device ID), household_id for CTV, campaign_id, creative_id, line_item_id, and the cross products (user × campaign), (user × creative), (household × campaign), (user × line_item). Pacing-side keys are bounded: campaign_id, line_item_id, advertiser_id.
domain_fit.window_semantics_required: Both. Sliding / hopping windows dominate for frequency-cap recency rules ('no more than 1 impression per hour', '3 per day, 10 per week') and for the pacing controller's 10-second / 1-minute feedback loops. Tumbling windows are required for IO-level lifetime / daily caps that reset at midnight in the advertiser's timezone. Exact aggregates are strongly preferred — overshooting a cap by even a few impressions can breach an IO and require make-goods — although CTV cross-device frequency caps already tolerate approximate de-duplication in practice. HLL / approximate sketches are usable on the pacing side (e.g. n_unique users reached per campaign) but NOT on the per-user count side.
domain_fit.exactly_once_or_idempotency_needs: Strict no-double-count on the cap side. Each billable impression must increment the (user × campaign) counter exactly once even though the bid_request, bid_win, win_notice, rendered-impression and billable-impression events arrive on different timelines and can be retried. Industry pattern is to key counters by bid_id and use the billable / win-notice event (not the bid_request) as the increment trigger, with idempotency by bid_id. Pacing-side counters tolerate at-least-once but the cap side does not. This is the hardest semantic in the domain.

technical_fit.latency_budget: Single-digit milliseconds end-to-end for the read on the bid path: the SSP/exchange typically gives the DSP ~100 ms total to return a bid (Google AdX deadline is 120 ms; Yospace's new server-guided ad-insertion (SGAI) measures bid-to-display at ~6 ms for CTV), and feature lookup is one slice of that. The de-facto industry target for per-feature get is sub-ms. beava's sub-ms TCP+msgpack get / batch_get sits comfortably inside this budget. Write latency is less critical — impression-counter writes happen off the hot path on the billable / win-notice callback.
technical_fit.feature_freshness_sla: Single-digit seconds at the absolute outermost, sub-second strongly preferred on the cap side (a campaign can burn through a daily cap in seconds during a creative refresh or a viral moment); ~10 s on the pacing side (Twitter / X publicly run their pacing-parameter recompute at 10 s intervals, and that is the de-facto industry cadence). beava's push-on-event no-broker model fits this directly — Aerospike, Redis and bespoke in-Rust services are the incumbents at the same freshness tier.
technical_fit.throughput_profile: Domain-wide: ~600-650 B bid requests/day across all major exchanges, peaks of 10-12 M QPS industry-aggregate, ~250 k QPS as a common DSP-capacity-planning number for global open-auction RTB. Per-buyer published numbers: The Trade Desk ~10 M QPS, Criteo ~20-25 M transactions/s (recently quoted at 290 M QPS aggregate on Aerospike), PubMatic / OpenX each >100-200 B bid requests/day, Index Exchange 50 B/day. Each bid request generates 1 cap read and (on win) 1 cap write, so write-EPS is ~win-rate × QPS (typically 0.1-10 %). One beava node at the published ~684 k EPS handles a single bidder / SSP region or a single mid-size CTV ad-server; tier-1 DSP / exchange aggregate volumes require horizontal partitioning that beava v0 does not yet do in-process. [uncertain]
technical_fit.read_to_write_ratio: Read-heavy on the bid path (every bid request reads cap state; only winning bids write). Typical industry win rate is 1-10 %, so read:write is roughly 10:1 to 100:1 on the cap-counter dataset. The pacing-spend counter is closer to balanced (one write per win, one read per pacing-cycle every 10 s). Strongly favours beava's batch_get path.
technical_fit.state_size_estimate: Dominated by (user × campaign) cardinality. A tier-1 DSP serves ~10^9 users × 10^4-10^5 active campaigns; not every pair is non-zero, but the live working set of (user × campaign) tuples with non-trivial counters is realistically 10^9-10^10, which at ~50-100 B per record (a few small counters + recency timestamps) is 50 GB-1 TB hot state. Mid-tier DSP / CTV ad-server: 10^8 households × 10^3-10^4 campaigns => 10 GB-100 GB hot state, which fits one beava box. Tier-1 scale does NOT fit one beava box in v0 and requires external hand-sharding. The Criteo public benchmark uses 20 Aerospike nodes for petabyte-scale RTB state. [uncertain]
technical_fit.cardinality_pattern: Bounded and small on campaigns / creatives / line items / advertisers (10^3-10^5). Slowly-growing on users (10^8-10^9 cookie-replacement era) and households (10^7-10^8 CTV). Explosive on the cross product (user × campaign), which is the actual cap key — this is the cardinality that drives memory budget. Cookie deprecation / Privacy Sandbox would shift the user-side cardinality from cookie IDs to Protected-Audience-style on-device counters, partially relieving server-side state for browser display but leaving CTV / mobile-app / authenticated-user inventory unchanged.
technical_fit.typical_state_lifecycle_and_ttl: Seconds to lifetime. Recency caps: minutes to hours. Daily caps: 24 h TTL with explicit reset at advertiser-timezone midnight. Weekly / lifetime caps: 7 d to campaign-duration (weeks to months). DV360 publicly retains user-exposure data for 90 days. Pacing state: ephemeral, tens of seconds. The 'forever' lifetime-cap counter is the longest-lived state and is the one that most pressures beava's in-memory-only model — it must survive node restarts via WAL+snapshot.
technical_fit.typical_feature_count_per_decision: 20-100+ features per bid decision (per-user-per-campaign count, per-user-per-creative count, per-household count for CTV, recency timestamps at multiple horizons, per-campaign pacing rates, win-rate, audience-segment features, pCTR/pCVR model inputs). Strongly favours batch_get — exactly what beava ships.
technical_fit.durability_requirements: Crash-safe is the right tier — billing-grade durability is NOT required because the system of record for billing is the exchange's win-notice / billable-impression log, not the DSP's cap counter. But the buyer cannot afford to lose hours of cap state in a crash — that would let a campaign overshoot its IO and either generate make-goods or breach contracted reach. beava's WAL + periodic snapshot is the right shape; the open question is cold-start replay time on 100+ GB of hot state and whether buyers tolerate the brief over-delivery during recovery. [uncertain]
technical_fit.deployment_topology_fit: Mixed fit. (a) Single-binary per region / per PoP is a strong fit for SSPs and CTV ad-servers (PubMatic publicly has 9 data centers; Aerospike's AdTech reference architectures are explicitly regional). (b) Single-binary per bidder shard is a reasonable fit for mid-sized DSPs that already hand-shard by user_id hash. (c) Tier-1 DSP global (TheTradeDesk, DV360, Criteo) is a poor fit for v0 — they need multi-region active-active replication with consistent counters across regions, which beava does not ship. The 'refuse-on-network-FS' rule is fine here (WAL on local NVMe is the standard pattern). The hard v0 limit is no in-process sharding.

commercial_fit.who_buys: Ad-server / bidder platform engineering teams at: (a) DSPs (The Trade Desk, DV360, Criteo, MediaMath-successor, StackAdapt, AdRoll, Basis, Yahoo DSP, MGID), (b) SSPs and ad exchanges (Magnite, PubMatic, OpenX, Index Exchange, Xandr/Microsoft, FreeWheel, SpringServe), (c) CTV ad-servers and FAST publishers (FreeWheel, SpringServe, Roku Ad Manager, Magnite Streaming, Yospace SGAI, fuboTV, Hulu/Disney ad-tech, Paramount, Warner Bros Discovery), (d) ad-tech vendors selling capping / pacing as a managed component (Kevel, AdGlare, AdButler, ShareChat-style in-house stacks), (e) large in-house growth / performance teams at retailers, classifieds and mobile-app networks running their own bidders. The buyer is platform engineering / ad-server engineering, not the media-buyer / trader who configures the cap.
commercial_fit.market_size_signal: Programmatic advertising market is in the high $100B - low $1T range depending on definition (eMarketer-adjacent estimates: ~$755B global programmatic spend in 2025; multiple vendor reports put 2025 programmatic at $834B and project >$3T by 2034-2035). Programmatic ad-platform software market specifically (Grand View Research) ~$8.4B in 2023, projected ~$41B by 2030 at 27% CAGR. Aerospike's public AdTech customer roster (Trade Desk, Criteo, MGID, fuboTV, Yahoo, AppLovin-adjacent) is direct evidence that the per-vendor infrastructure spend is large. Criteo's published Aerospike migration cut hardware cost by ~78 % from the prior Couchbase+Memcached stack — that is the size of the opportunity for a more efficient feature backend. [uncertain]
commercial_fit.urgency_drivers: 1) Cookie-deprecation timeline whiplash: Chrome reversed third-party-cookie deprecation in April 2025, and Google formally dissolved the Privacy Sandbox initiative in October 2025 — Protected Audience / Topics / ARA are still functional but now optional rather than mandatory, leaving the industry to maintain BOTH cookie-based and on-device cap stacks in parallel, which doubles complexity and creates pull for a flexible feature backend. 2) CTV growth (linear-to-streaming shift) is creating a fresh wave of ad-server builds in 2024-2026 (SpringServe Next-Gen closed beta with Disney / Paramount / Roku / Samsung / Warner Bros Discovery in April 2025, FreeWheel-Magnite integration April 2025) — these are greenfield infrastructure decisions where a single-binary feature server is in scope. 3) Cost pressure: Criteo's 78 % hardware reduction via a better feature backend is a case study that every CFO can read. 4) Sustainability / carbon-cost arguments (Criteo also cited 80 % carbon-footprint reduction). 5) Open-source pull: incumbents are commercial (Aerospike, Redis Enterprise) or DIY-in-Rust — a permissively-licensed Apache-2.0 single binary is a credible alternative for the long tail of mid-sized DSPs / SSPs / CTV ad-servers.
commercial_fit.regulatory_or_audit_constraints: GDPR (user IDs and household IDs are personal data; argues for short TTLs, hashed IDs, on-device wherever possible — Protected Audience-style on-device frequency caps are an explicit GDPR-friendly direction), CCPA / CPRA and state-by-state US privacy laws (require opt-out plumbing and limit retention), DSA / DMA (for EU gatekeepers), and the IAB TCF / GPP consent frameworks (the DSP / SSP must check consent state on every bid). Industry data-retention norm is 12-24 months for personal data; DV360 retains user-exposure data 90 days. There is also an audit / reach-measurement dimension: MRC viewability standards (50 % pixels / 1 s display / 2 s video) define what counts as a 'counted impression', which in turn defines when the cap counter increments. PCI-DSS / SOX do not apply directly. beava's v0 lack of TLS / auth is a blocker for any production deployment exposed beyond a private VPC.
commercial_fit.time_to_value_signal: Fast for the demo: the beava/python/beava/demos/adtech demo already ships (Impression, Click, Conversion) events with (user_id, campaign_id) keys — adding a @bv.table that counts impressions per (user × campaign) over (1h, 24h, 7d, lifetime) is a one-afternoon job and would produce a working frequency-cap microbenchmark. 1-3 days to a runnable end-to-end demo (bidder mock + cap-check + pacing-feature read) on a laptop. 2-6 weeks to a production pilot at a mid-sized DSP or CTV ad-server once TLS / auth / sharding gaps below are addressed. 3-9 months to displace Aerospike at a tier-1 DSP — beava is not there in v0.

competition.incumbents: Aerospike is the dominant incumbent for ad-tech feature / profile / cap storage (public customers: The Trade Desk, Criteo, MGID, fuboTV, Yahoo) with sub-ms reads, petabyte-scale benchmarks on ~20 nodes, and multi-region active-active. Redis (and Redis Enterprise / Elasticache) is the default for smaller deployments and for the in-cluster cap-counter pattern (Bhaumik Shukla and ankushs92 blogs document the standard 'master + per-bidder read replicas' frequency-cap topology). ScyllaDB / Cassandra and Couchbase appear in the historical Criteo / Yahoo stacks. Apache Flink / RisingWave / Materialize are used for the analytics / pacing-analytics half of the stack but not the inline cap-check path. In-house Rust / C++ services on top of RocksDB / Sled (Cloudflare-style, Criteo's Couchbase-replacement era) are common at the top end. AWS publishes a managed reference architecture ('Guidance for Building a Real Time Bidder for Advertising on AWS') anchored on Aerospike and ElastiCache.
competition.competitive_incumbent_per_domain: Domain-specific: Aerospike (overwhelming default for DSP / SSP / exchange feature + cap stores), Redis Enterprise (the broad mid-market default — see the AWS Architecture Blog 'Serving Billions of Ads in Just 100 ms Using Amazon Elasticache (Redis OSS)'), Kevel (managed ad server with built-in capping for retail-media / API-first), AdGlare / AdButler (smaller ad servers with capping), SpringServe / FreeWheel (CTV ad-server with built-in capping at the household level), Yospace SGAI (server-guided CTV ad-insertion with frequency awareness), Google Ad Manager / DV360 (built-in capping for buy-side), The Trade Desk's internal Koa stack (uses Aerospike), Criteo's internal stack (uses Aerospike, migrated from Couchbase + Memcached). Privacy Sandbox Protected Audience is a parallel on-device alternative that moves the cap counter off the server entirely — beava and its incumbents are all server-side stacks that compete in the non-Privacy-Sandbox part of the market (CTV, mobile-app, authenticated-user, non-Chrome).
competition.beava_differentiator: 1) Single binary with no Kafka / Flink / Redis-cluster ceremony — credibly fits the smaller-DSP, CTV-publisher, and regional-SSP topology. 2) 50+ aggregation primitives natively cover counters, velocity, distribution, recency / distance — exactly the cap-and-pacing primitive set, without writing Lua (Redis) or UDFs (Aerospike). 3) Sub-ms TCP+msgpack get / batch_get matches the inline bid-path latency budget. 4) Apache-2.0, no open-core, no SaaS lock-in — meaningful versus Aerospike's per-node enterprise licence and Redis Enterprise's licensing. 5) Push-on-event model maps directly to how a bidder already produces win-notice / billable-impression events — no broker hop. 6) Per-key TTL and explicit window semantics built in, versus rolling-your-own with Redis TTLs and Lua. 7) The adtech demo already ships in /python/beava/demos/adtech with realistic Impression / Click / Conversion events — the on-ramp for evaluators is short.
competition.where_beava_loses_today: 1) No TLS, no auth on :8080/:8081/:8090 — disqualifying for any production deployment outside a tightly controlled VPC; impossible to run as a managed service or in a multi-tenant SSP cluster as-is. 2) No in-process sharding — single-binary v0 caps out at ~684 k EPS / one box of RAM, which is fine for a mid-size CTV publisher or a regional SSP but is 10-100x short of tier-1 DSP / exchange aggregate scale. 3) No multi-region active-active replication of counters — frequency caps for a global advertiser must be consistent across regions or the cap leaks across regions; Aerospike's XDR (Cross-Datacenter Replication) is the explicit incumbent feature here. 4) No native cross-key idempotency / dedup-by-bid_id — the buyer has to ensure each billable-impression event increments the (user × campaign) cap exactly once across retries; today that has to be implemented above beava. 5) No triggers / 'fire when counter crosses cap' — pacing wants 'when campaign spend velocity exceeds budget rate, dial down bid multiplier' as an event-driven action, not as a poll. 6) No multi-tenancy primitives (namespaces, per-tenant quotas) — a managed-bidder SaaS or an SSP serving many DSPs needs this. 7) Cold-start replay time on 100+ GB of hot cap state is unbenchmarked in v0; a node restart during an active campaign is an effective outage. 8) No built-in MRC viewability / billable-impression timing model — the buyer has to model 'cap counter increments on viewable, not on rendered' above beava. 9) Limited public adtech case study — Aerospike has Trade Desk and Criteo on the record; beava has none yet.
competition.integration_surface: Producers: bidder process (Rust / Go / Java / C++) emitting bid_request, bid_win, billable_imp events on the hot path; SSP / exchange win-notice / billing-notice callback (HTTP) emitting the authoritative billable event; CTV ad-server emitting household-keyed impressions; pacing-service callback (e.g. the Twitter-style 10-s recompute) reading per-campaign velocity features. beava's HTTP/JSON :8080 fits the win-notice callback shape; TCP+msgpack :8081 fits the hot-path bidder push. Consumers: the bidder itself reading caps on the bid path via batch_get; the pacing controller reading per-campaign features every 1-10 s; pCTR / pCVR ML scorers (XGBoost / LightGBM / ONNX, usually a sidecar process) consuming the same per-(user × campaign) features. Notably DIFFERENT from Kafka-first feature stores (Tecton, Feast, Chalk, Fennel) which assume a Kafka producer — beava's push surface is closer to the bidder's native shape.
competition.scoring_engine_coupling: Both, with a clean seam. Frequency-cap enforcement is a deterministic rule (count >= cap => suppress) read directly from beava. Pacing is a control-loop algorithm (PID / multiplicative / bang-bang / Twitter's pacing-library) that LIVES IN A SEPARATE SERVICE and READS beava counters every 10 s. pCTR / pCVR is an ML scorer (XGBoost / DNN) that also reads beava as a feature backend. beava sits below all three and exposes the same per-entity primitives to each.

adoption_signals.existing_public_users_or_case_studies: No public beava users in ad-tech yet. [uncertain] Comparable production systems: The Trade Desk (Aerospike, ~10 M QPS), Criteo (Aerospike, 20-25 M tx/s, 290 M QPS aggregate, 78 % hardware reduction vs Couchbase+Memcached), fuboTV (Aerospike, frequency-capping migration from Redis), MGID (Aerospike), Twitter / X (in-house pacing-library service, public blog 2021), Snap (in-house, public service-mesh blog), ShareChat (public Medium blog on PID-controller budget pacing), Roku (public PID-controller pacing blog), AWS RTB Fabric (managed reference architecture). Open-source DSPs / bidders that could be plumbed onto beava: RTB4FREE (Java, OpenRTB 2.x, ~25 k QPS / node), RTBkit (older, C++), vanilla-rtb / rapid-bidder (C++14), seanZhang414/openadserver (Python / FastAPI / PyTorch with built-in CTR prediction).
adoption_signals.community_discussions: No beava-specific Discord / GitHub Discussion threads on frequency capping or pacing identified in this snapshot. [uncertain] Adjacent active community signals: AdExchanger and Digiday coverage of Privacy Sandbox dissolution (October 2025), Hacker News threads on Aerospike vs Redis cost, Twitter/X Engineering Dec-2021 pacing-service blog, Snap Engineering service-mesh writeups, ShareChat TechByte on Medium, multiple academic / arXiv pacing-control papers (Smart Pacing 2015, Twitter Bucketized Hysteresis 2022, Snap Feedback Control 2025), and the wnzhang/rtb-papers GitHub list which is the canonical bibliography for this domain.
adoption_signals.examples_or_demos_in_repo: Yes — /tmp/docker-desktop-root/run/desktop/mnt/host/d/Code/Beava/beava/python/beava/demos/adtech/ ships a 10 000-event synthetic dataset (events.jsonl) with Impression / Click / Conversion events keyed by (user_id, campaign_id) and a schema.json declaring those event types. A dedicated, named 'frequency-capping & pacing' vertical demo — with @bv.table aggregations for per-(user × campaign) caps and per-campaign pacing velocities, plus a mock bidder doing batch_get — does NOT appear to exist as of the snapshot reviewed. [uncertain] This is a one-afternoon authoring gap, not a structural one.
adoption_signals.adversarial_pressure_level: Low to moderate. This is a passive-load domain, not an actively adversarial one — the counter-parties are honest exchanges and bidders, not attackers. The 'pressure' comes from scale (10^9-10^10 (user × campaign) cells), tight latency (1-10 ms), and IO-grade no-double-count semantics, not from adversaries trying to subvert the cap. Feature drift is slow: the underlying capping primitive (count per cross-product over time window) is decades stable; what changes is the entity-grain (cookie => Protected-Audience ID => household ID for CTV). Lower adversarial pressure than fraud / bot defence means beava has more design-time stability here but also less of the 'developer ergonomics for fast feature iteration' selling point — the buyer optimizes for cost, latency and operational simplicity, not for time-to-add-a-new-feature.

risk_and_non_goals.non_goals: 1) Multi-region active-active counter consistency — beava v0 cannot guarantee a global campaign's frequency cap is consistent across regions, which is table-stakes for tier-1 global DSPs / exchanges. They keep using Aerospike XDR. 2) Petabyte-scale state on commodity hardware — Criteo's 1 PB-on-20-nodes Aerospike benchmark is out of reach for a single-binary in-memory beava box. 3) Long-historical lookback / batch backfill for attribution modelling — that is a lakehouse / Parquet job, not a beava job. 4) Cross-entity joins ('show me all campaigns where users overlap with audience X') — that's an OLAP / graph problem. 5) Acting as the bidder or the pacing controller itself — beava is the feature backend underneath both. 6) Acting as the win-notice / billing-event system of record — that is the exchange's responsibility. 7) Acting as the audience-graph / identity-resolution layer (LiveRamp / The Trade Desk UID2 / Google ID stitching) — those are upstream of beava and supply the entity_id. 8) Browser-side / on-device frequency capping under Privacy Sandbox Protected Audience — that is by-design on-device and not a server-side feature-store opportunity. 9) Heavy ML training — beava feeds online inference, not training.
risk_and_non_goals.open_engineering_gaps: Concrete features beava would need to ship to be production-grade for this domain, roughly in priority order: 1) TLS termination and mutual TLS on :8081 / :8090, plus a token / mTLS auth model on the admin and push surfaces — without this, no SSP / DSP can deploy beava outside a private VPC. 2) In-process sharding by entity-key prefix (user_id hash or campaign_id hash) so a single tenant beyond ~684 k EPS or ~50-100 GB hot state can scale within one cluster without external hand-sharding. 3) Cross-region replication of counters (CRDT-style merge or XDR-style log shipping) — frequency caps for a global advertiser must be consistent across regions; this is the single biggest gap versus Aerospike. 4) Idempotency / dedup-by-event-id primitive — the buyer needs first-class 'increment (user × campaign) counter once per bid_id' semantics so that bid_request / bid_win / win_notice / rendered / billable retries do not double-count. 5) Triggers / 'callback when counter crosses cap' — for the pacing-side control loop and for inline cap-enforcement actions. 6) Multi-tenancy: per-tenant namespaces, per-tenant quotas, per-tenant rate-limit accounting so a managed-bidder SaaS or an SSP serving many DSPs can isolate customers. 7) Per-key TTL with explicit window semantics tied to advertiser-timezone midnight resets (24 h / 7 d caps that roll over consistently across nodes). 8) Cold-start WAL-replay time benchmark and bounded SLA for 50-200 GB hot state — a node restart during an active campaign must not become an outage. 9) An MRC-viewability-aware billable-event documented pattern — when the cap counter increments must be configurable (rendered vs viewable vs billable). 10) Native support for Protected Audience / on-device-counter integration (e.g. accept periodic batched event updates from on-device APIs) — a hedge against the 2025-onwards privacy-API churn. 11) A streaming admin / debug surface to let ad-ops query 'top-k campaigns by spend velocity in the last 60 s' and 'campaigns within 90 % of daily cap right now' without materializing the full keyspace. 12) A documented, benchmarked frequency-capping + pacing reference architecture and an /examples vertical demo (the events.jsonl is there, the @bv.table demo isn't yet).
risk_and_non_goals.trigger_action_required: Yes — pacing is fundamentally event-driven ('when campaign X's 60-s impression rate exceeds its IO-derived target by 20 %, dial bid multiplier down'). Today a buyer has to poll per-campaign velocity features every 10 s from a separate pacing service (the Twitter / X pattern). A first-class 'trigger on threshold' primitive in beava would let the pacing controller run as a callback rather than a polling loop, which is meaningful at the campaign-count scale (10^4-10^5). Cap enforcement on the bid path does NOT need triggers — the read happens on every bid anyway — but cap-breach alerting and pacing both do.
